# SK2054 — A signed modulus result is compared for equality with a non-zero value

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `%` on a possibly-negative signed operand is compared with `==` or `!=` against a non-zero constant, so the test fails for every value of the wrong sign.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S2197 |

## Why

⚠ C# gives `%` the sign of the dividend: `-5 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. So `x % 2 == 1` is false for every negative odd `x`, and the parity check that reads as obviously correct is wrong on half its domain. ⚠ `x % 2 == 0` is **not** reported and must never be: zero has no sign, so comparing against it is correct for both signs — a rule that reported it would be wrong about the one spelling that is right. There is no fix, because the repair depends on what was meant: `!= 0` for a parity test, `Math.Abs(x % n) == k` for a magnitude test, and `x % n == k || x % n == -k` where both signs are wanted.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
bool IsOdd(int value) => value % 2 == 1;
```

Write:

```csharp
bool IsOdd(int value) => value % 2 != 0;
```

## When it does not fire

Reported only when the `%` result type is a signed fixed-width integral type, the comparison constant is not zero, and the dividend is not already proven non-negative. ⚠ The dividend is taken as non-negative when its own type is unsigned (`byte`, `ushort`, `uint`, `ulong`, `char` — so `someByte % 2 == 1` is correct and not reported even though the operation promotes to `int`), when it is a non-negative constant, when it is a collection count or a length, or when it is `Math.Abs`/`MathF.Abs`. Floating-point `%`, user-defined operators, lifted comparisons, native integers and `is` patterns over a modulus are outside this initial scope. Where a caller genuinely only ever passes non-negative values the finding is a true statement about the expression and a false alarm about the program; the repair is the same either way.
